subject: English
passage: The telegraph dispatch is a signal of words transmitted upon the wire, composed for immediate purpose and persists no longer than the brevity of reception can preserve it; but a letter inscribed is a document, remaining in every man's cabinet, always ready to renew its acquaintance with his recollection, and always ready to be produced as testament or witness to any account he renders from it, and preserves its sentiments through generations hence, to the perpetuity of earthly time, when the correspondent is forgotten in his grave.
prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: People are less likely to forget a message when they receive it by telegraph than they are when they read it in a letter.
choices.B: Messages preserved in written letters have a greater permanence than communications that are merely transmitted by telegraph.
choices.C: Most correspondents have little expectation of being remembered well past their lifetimes.
choices.D: Unless a telegraph dispatch is transmitted with proper technical precision, it may be misunderstood.

explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it captures the central thesis running throughout the passage: written letters possess greater permanence than telegraph communications. The text develops this through an extended contrast. Telegraph dispatches are described as ephemeral, persisting 'no longer than the brevity of reception can preserve it' and 'composed for immediate purpose,' while letters are characterized as permanent documents remaining 'in every man's cabinet' and preserving sentiments 'through generations hence, to the perpetuity of earthly time.' The structure moves from the temporary telegraph to the enduring letter (introduced with contrasting 'but'), establishing permanence as the organizing principle.
